```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A literature that grew as fast as research on COVID-19 and education is
difficult to survey by reading. Thousands of abstracts appeared within a few
years, written in different disciplines and for different audiences, and a
map of their themes has to be built from the texts themselves. A semantic
topic model builds that map from meaning rather than from shared words: each
abstract becomes a sentence embedding, a vector in which texts with similar
meaning lie close together, and a topic is a group of nearby embeddings. The
topics are then read through their most typical texts, and words serve only
as labels.

Abstracts pose a problem of granularity. An abstract is several sentences
that do different jobs (context, aim, sample, method, finding, implication),
and an encoder reads a limited number of tokens: the default model,
`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, reads at most 256 and ignores the rest. A whole abstract is
therefore one vector for a mixture of statements, part of which the model
never sees, while a sentence is short enough to be read in full but carries
only one of those statements. This case study fits topics at both levels and
asks what each level finds: what the abstracts are about, what their
sentences do, how the two groupings relate, and which to use for which
question.

Unlike the vignettes, this article downloads a model and encodes several
thousand abstracts and all of their sentences, which takes a few minutes. The
numbers in the text are computed when the article is built, so they always
describe the output shown.

```{r package}
library(sbert)
```

## Data

`covid` holds `r nrow(covid)` records of peer-reviewed research on COVID-19
and its effects on education, children, schools, and society, published from
`r with(covid, min(Year))` to `r with(covid, max(Year))`. Each row is one
record.

- **Publication year:** `Year`, an integer; available for every record.
- **Text:** `Abstract`, the abstract, the unit of analysis. Records without an
  abstract carry the placeholder `"[No abstract available]"`.

`r nrow(subset(covid, Abstract == "[No abstract available]"))` records have
only the placeholder. They are dropped, and the remaining abstracts are
counted by year.

```{r data}
abstracts <- subset(covid, Abstract != "[No abstract available]")
nrow(abstracts)
xtabs(~ Year, data = abstracts)
with(abstracts, sum(grepl("©", Abstract)))
```

`r nrow(abstracts)` abstracts remain, most of them from
`r names(which.max(xtabs(~ Year, data = abstracts)))`, and
`r with(abstracts, sum(grepl("©", Abstract)))` of them contain a "©" sign.

Almost every abstract ends with a copyright notice, such as "© 2021 Informa UK
Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group." Left in, the notices would form
topics of their own, grouped by publisher rather than by research. The
`remove` argument of `clean_corpus()` deletes text that matches a regular
expression. The pattern below deletes a notice at the end of an abstract that
starts with "©", "Copyright ©", or "Copyright" and a year; abstracts that
mention copyright as a subject keep their text. `clean_corpus()` also repairs
broken characters, removes HTML tags, URLs, DOIs, and bracketed citations,
and with `min_content = 0.5` drops rows that are mostly numbers or symbols
rather than words. Given a data frame and a `column`, it cleans that column
and keeps the other columns.

```{r clean}
abstracts <- clean_corpus(
  abstracts,
  column = "Abstract",
  remove = "(copyright:?\\s*(©|\\d{4})|©).{0,1000}$",
  min_content = 0.5
)
nrow(abstracts)
with(abstracts, sum(grepl("©", Abstract)))
```

All `r nrow(abstracts)` abstracts pass the content filter, and after
cleaning `r with(abstracts, sum(grepl("©", Abstract)))` contain a "©" sign.
`dedupe()` counts the distinct texts:

```{r distinct}
nrow(dedupe(abstracts, column = "Abstract"))
```

`r nrow(dedupe(abstracts, column = "Abstract"))` of the
`r nrow(abstracts)` abstracts are distinct; the others repeat an abstract
that appears in another record. Every record is kept, so a repeated abstract
counts once per record in the topic sizes below.

The last property that matters for the model is length. The number of words
per abstract and the number of sentences that `segment()` finds:

```{r length}
with(abstracts, summary(lengths(strsplit(Abstract, "\\s+"))))
sentences <- with(abstracts, segment(Abstract, level = "sentence"))
nrow(sentences)
```

The median abstract has
`r with(abstracts, median(lengths(strsplit(Abstract, "\\s+"))))` words, and
`r with(abstracts, round(100 * mean(lengths(strsplit(Abstract, "\\s+")) > 200)))`%
of the abstracts have more than 200. A tokenizer emits more tokens than
words, so these abstracts are likely to exceed the 256 tokens that the model
reads, and their endings, where findings and conclusions usually stand, do
not enter the whole-abstract embedding. The `r nrow(sentences)` sentences, about
`r round(nrow(sentences) / nrow(abstracts), 1)` per abstract, are each read in
full.

## Fitting abstracts and sentences

Install the ONNX Runtime and download the default model,
`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`. Both steps happen once per computer.

```{r runtime}
install_runtime()
model_download()
```

Words such as *covid*, *pandemic*, and *study* appear in nearly every
abstract, so they are added to the standard English stop words, and
`numbers = "remove"` leaves out bare numbers such as years. Stop words affect
only the word labels and the word-based measures; the topics themselves are
computed from the embeddings of the full text.

```{r stop-words}
covid_stop_words <- stop_words(add = c(
  "covid", "coronavirus", "sars", "cov", "pandemic", "disease",
  "study", "studies", "result", "results", "conclusion", "conclusions",
  "background", "method", "methods", "objective", "aim"
))
```

`compare_topics()` fits one model for each candidate number of topics, here
on whole abstracts (`"document"`) and on sentences (`"sentence"`) in one
call. `max_tokens = 200` caps a sentence at 200 of the model's tokens and
splits a longer one at its punctuation, so that no sentence is cut off.
`coherence_weight = "size"` averages the coherence of a candidate's topics in
proportion to their sizes. A topic of a handful of unusual abstracts whose
rare words always occur together scores a very high coherence and, in an
unweighted mean, can make a candidate look better than its other topics
justify; in the run published with sbert 0.5.12, a three-abstract topic at
eight topics had a coherence of 0.90 and lifted the unweighted mean of that
candidate to 0.18. k-means on tens of thousands of sentences can need more
than the default 100 iterations to settle; `iter_max = 300` gives it room,
and the `converged` column of the table reports whether every candidate
converged.

```{r sweep}
sweep <- compare_topics(
  abstracts,
  column = "Abstract",
  n_topics = c(4, 6, 8, 10, 12),
  segment = c("document", "sentence"),
  max_tokens = 200,
  coherence_weight = "size",
  iter_max = 300,
  stop_words = covid_stop_words,
  numbers = "remove"
)
sweep
summary(sweep)
```

The table has one row per level and candidate: `coherence` (how often the top
words of a topic occur together), `topic_diversity` (the share of distinct
words among all topics' top words), `explained` (the share of the variance in
the embeddings that lies between topics), and `converged`. `summary()` gives
the most coherent candidate at each level. The plot shows the three measures
against the number of topics:

```{r sweep-plot}
plot(sweep)
```

`explained` tends to rise as topics are added, so it cannot choose a count
by itself; coherence and diversity can. To compare
the two levels at the same resolution, both are read at eight topics below.
The guide [Choosing the number of topics and the
granularity](choosing-topics.html) discusses the choice in detail.

```{r models}
topic_model <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 8, segment = "document")
sentence_model <- fitted(sweep, n_topics = 8, segment = "sentence")
```

## What are the abstracts about?

`representatives()` returns, for each topic, the abstracts closest to that
topic and clearly farther from every other topic. One per topic, in full:

```{r representatives}
knitr::kable(representatives(topic_model, n = 1), digits = 2)
```

The plot shows the opening of two abstracts per topic:

```{r plot-representatives, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 9}
plot(topic_model, type = "representatives", n_representatives = 2)
```

A topic is named from what its representatives share: the population studied
(students, teachers, children, residents), the setting (schools,
universities, laboratories, hospitals), or the kind of paper (survey,
reflection, editorial). Two abstracts that use the same words can fall in
different topics when they report different things, and the representatives,
not the word lists below, show which. `topic_sizes()` counts the abstracts in
each topic:

```{r sizes}
topic_sizes(topic_model)
```

The `r nrow(as.data.frame(topic_model))` abstracts are divided into eight
topics; the largest holds
`r with(topic_sizes(topic_model), max(n_documents))` and the smallest
`r with(topic_sizes(topic_model), min(n_documents))`. A very small topic is
worth reading in full: it can isolate papers that do not belong to the
corpus's subject, which is useful in itself. `summary()` lists each topic
under its label with its size and the coherence of its top words, and
`terms()` lists those words:

```{r summary}
summary(topic_model)
terms(topic_model, n = 5)
```

Words such as *online*, *learning*, and *students* run through the whole
corpus, so several topics share them, and a topic's top words describe it
less precisely than its representatives. The embeddings separate abstracts by
what they report rather than by the words they use, and the word lists serve
as labels after the topics have been read.

## What do the sentences do?

The sentence model was fitted in the same call. It models
`r nrow(as.data.frame(sentence_model))` sentences. Its representatives are
short enough to read in full:

```{r sentence-representatives}
knitr::kable(representatives(sentence_model, n = 3), digits = 2)
```

Sentence topics can be of two kinds. Some are subjects, as at the document
level. Others gather sentences that play the same part in an
abstract whatever its subject: the opening that states what the pandemic did
to education, the report of a sample and response rate, the description of a
method, a general or hedging statement. In the run published with sbert
0.5.12, one sentence topic was represented by sentences such as "Results: Of
268 students enrolled, 104 responded" and another by "Content analysis
technique was used in the analysis of the data obtained.", topics of
reporting rather than of research subjects.

A sentence topic that plays a structural part appears in many abstracts.
`topic_sizes(by = "document")` counts the abstracts that have at least one
sentence in each topic:

```{r sentence-sizes}
topic_sizes(sentence_model, by = "document")
```

`proportion` is here the share of abstracts that touch the topic, so the
shares do not add up to one. The most widespread sentence topic reaches
`r with(topic_sizes(sentence_model, by = "document"), round(100 * max(proportion)))`%
of the abstracts. `summary()` reports the sentence topics' top words and
coherence:

```{r sentence-summary}
summary(sentence_model)
```

The words of a structural topic describe its function only indirectly: no
word says that a sentence opens an abstract or reports a sample. The
representatives remain the evidence.

## How do the two granularities differ?

`topic_gamma()` gives the mix of sentence topics within each abstract: the
share of its sentences that fall in each topic. With `top = 2` it keeps the
two largest shares of every abstract:

```{r gamma}
head(topic_gamma(sentence_model, top = 2), 10)
```

An abstract whose largest share is close to one says one kind of thing
throughout; an abstract whose largest share is well below one spreads its
sentences over several topics, which a single whole-abstract topic cannot
show. To relate the two groupings, each abstract's document topic is paired
with its dominant sentence topic (`top = 1`; an abstract whose sentences are
split evenly is counted under one of the tied topics), and the pairs are
cross-tabulated:

```{r crosstab}
granularity <- merge(
  as.data.frame(topic_model),
  topic_gamma(sentence_model, top = 1),
  by = "document_id",
  suffixes = c("_abstract", "_sentence")
)
xtabs(~ topic_abstract + topic_sentence, data = granularity)
```

Each row is a whole-abstract topic and each column the sentence topic that
holds the largest share of an abstract's sentences. A row concentrated in one
column means the abstract topic corresponds to one sentence topic; a row
spread across columns means that abstracts of one subject are dominated by
different kinds of sentences, typically the structural ones, which recur
across subjects. The most frequent dominant sentence topic is the dominant
one in
`r with(granularity, round(100 * max(prop.table(table(topic_sentence)))))`%
of the `r nrow(granularity)` abstracts.

## Which granularity to use

The two models answer different questions:

- **Whole abstracts** group papers by what each abstract is about as a
  whole. Use them to map the research themes of a literature. The model reads only the first 256 tokens, so the subject is
  taken mostly from the opening of a long abstract.
- **Sentences** group by what a single sentence says or does, and can yield
  structural topics (context, sample, method) next to subject topics. Use them to study how
  abstracts are written, to reach content beyond the first 256 tokens, or to
  describe each abstract as a mixture of topics with `topic_gamma()`.

Next steps:

- `predict(topic_model, new_abstracts)` assigns new abstracts to these topics
  without refitting; for the sentence model it splits the new abstracts into
  sentences in the same way. See [Assigning new documents and topic
  mixtures](assigning-topics.html).
- `reduce_topics(topic_model, n_topics = 4)` merges similar topics, and
  `topic_hierarchy()` shows which topics are closest to each other.
- [Segmenting long documents](segmenting.html) covers the sentence, clause,
  and phrase levels and `max_tokens`; [Preparing and cleaning a
  corpus](preparing-corpus.html) covers `clean_corpus()`.
- [Parallel and high-throughput topic modeling](parallel.html) shows how to
  encode once and reuse the embeddings across many fits and sessions.
